newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to assure G7 partners of continued growth.
newsitem.headline: Japan to assure G7 partners of continued growth.

text.p: Japan will likely assure its G7 partners this weekend that its economy is growing well, its contentious trade surplus won't rise much more, and of its resolve to correct the recent weakness of the yen.

But economists doubt if Tokyo can offer the kind of stimulus steps other nations would like to see, and if it can succeed in the difficult task of achieving a moderate fall of the dollar against the yen rather than a rapid one.
A sharp rise of the yen would run counter to Japan's current policy of ensuring economic growth, which is threatened by an increase in its sales tax on April 1.
The yen's weakness is helping Japan's economy by giving firms such as carmakers a competitive edge in world markets.

Much of the discussion at Sunday's meeting in Washington of the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- is expected to dwell on exchange rates.

Washington has voiced concern about a rise in the U.S. trade deficit with Japan, which Tokyo fears will keep climbing unless the dollar is pushed lower against the yen from the current level of around 126 yen.
The dollar has risen against other major currencies, especially the yen, since the G7 declared two years ago that the dollar had fallen too far.
Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. rose 11.2 percent to 379.8 billion yen ($3.04 billion) in March, the sixth consecutive month in which it had risen year-on-year.
"It would be unfortunate if Japan's surplus were again to become a major asymmetry in the world economy," Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said this week.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday that Japan would tell its partners in G7 that there is no need to worry about Japan's trade surplus mounting.

"Japan is in a tough position. I think the exchange rate is now at the limit of a comfort zone for both Japan and the United States. They (Japanese policy-makers) prefer the yen to be weak rather than strong because of the economy," said Lehman Brothers chief economist Russell Jones.
Economists said what Japan can do now to stimulate its economy is limited, as it is committed to sticking to fiscal tightening due to a huge budget deficit.
"Japan cannot offer anything new to prop up the economy except for reaffirming its continued efforts to carry out deregulation," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute Corp.

Currency operators in Tokyo say they expect the G7 to reiterate what it said at its last meeting in February in Berlin -- that the dollar's rise since April 1995 has ended. Mere repetition of the February statement could push up the dollar towards a 56-month high of 127.16 yen recorded in Tokyo on April 10.
Economists said Japan is likely to intervene in currency markets to halt a higher dollar, either alone or in cooperation with other G7 members.

A senior Finance Ministry official told Reuters last week that the G7 is likely to reaffirm the basics of the Berlin statement, but currency movements right up until Sunday could determine the actual wording of a G7 currency statement.

Fuji's Takagi said: "I don't expect G7 to issue a stronger currency statement like singling out the yen's rate against the dollar, but during the course of G7 discussion they may talk about possible concerted intervention."
